system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2156-11-26 04:23:00 to 2156-12-01 17:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of recurrent abdominal pain, gastroparesis, functional dyspepsia, anxiety, depression, PTSD, and hearing loss was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain following a switch from metoclopramide to erythromycin. Labs showed mild lipase elevation that resolved, ruling out acute pancreatitis. She was managed with bowel rest, IV fluids, and gradual advancement to a soft diet. The pain service recommended increasing gabapentin to reduce reliance on narcotics, and she transitioned successfully to oral pain control. Her nausea improved with medication adjustments, and she tolerated oral intake. She was discharged home with an increased dose of gabapentin, continued erythromycin, a short supply of hydromorphone, and follow-up planned with her gastroenterologist to manage ongoing motility issues and reduce future hospitalizations.
problems: Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

Gastrointestinal Tract:  The GI tract is of normal caliber throughout. No
mural thickening or abnormal enhancement.

Lymph Nodes: No significant mesenteric, retroperitoneal or porta hepatis
lymphadenopathy by size criteria.

Vasculature: The visualized abdominal aorta and proximal mesenteric vessels
appear patent without any significant areas of narrowing or dilatation.

Osseous and Soft Tissue Structures: The bone marrow demonstrates normal signal

1.  No biliary or acute pancreatic pathology.
2.  The pancreatic parenchyma demonstrates slightly less than typically

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospital doctors. You’re here because of abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It’s that same pain I always get—right in the middle, under my ribs. It’s been worse the last two days. I couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had this kind of pain many times before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Over fifty times. I’ve been in the hospital so often, I know the staff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve reviewed your records. We checked your blood in the ER and found your lipase was elevated—453—so we’re watching for pancreas issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it pancreatitis again? But I don’t drink, and I’ve had scans before that were normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re being careful. We did an ultrasound already—no gallstones, which is good. We’ll do an MRCP tomorrow to look more closely at your pancreas and ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want the pain to stop. I can’t take much more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help with that. For now, we’re keeping you on IV fluids and holding off on food to let your gut rest. We’ll start with clear liquids once things settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds? I take gabapentin, imipramine, and the erythromycin for my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing all your regular medications. The erythromycin might be causing some diarrhea, but we’ll keep it for now unless it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had diarrhea the past few days. Could that be from the erythromycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. We checked and you don’t have a fever or high white count, so it’s unlikely to be an infection like C. diff. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your MRCP results are back. There’s no sign of acute pancreatitis or blockage in the bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a flare-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acute, no. But there are signs of chronic changes—your pancreatic duct is a bit widened, and the tissue looks slightly altered. This fits with long-term irritation, possibly from past episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s chronic pancreatitis again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re calling it acute on chronic—meaning your long-standing condition flared up. But there’s no new damage or blockage. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not worse. Can I start eating soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll start with clear liquids today—broth, apple juice—and if you do well, move to full liquids tomorrow, then soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain? The hydromorphone helps, but I don’t want to rely on it too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping your gabapentin and imipramine going—they help with nerve-type pain and may reduce the need for narcotics over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My therapist said those help with the emotional side too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we had a therapist visit you yesterday. I’m glad that was helpful. Stress and pain often go together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had broth and jello yesterday and kept it down. Still a little bloated, but the pain is way less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll advance you to a soft diet today—things like toast, rice, applesauce. Let’s see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have soup with bread?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s fine. Just small portions at first. And keep taking the prochlorperazine if you feel nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’ve made it through two days of soft foods without vomiting or severe pain. Your diarrhea has also improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. I even slept through the night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll keep you on the same meds and plan for discharge in a day or two if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another scan soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your MRCP was recent and clear. We’ll leave follow-up to your gastroenterologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You had a full breakfast and lunch yesterday with no issues. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If the pain comes back severely, or you can’t keep food down, please call your doctor or go to the ER. Otherwise, stick to your regular meds and diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the hydromorphone? I only take it when the pain is really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, use it as needed, but try to rely more on gabapentin and imipramine. They’re safer for long-term use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Should I see my therapist more often?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good idea. Emotional health plays a big role in chronic pain. Keep up with your mental health care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially ready to go home. Your exam is normal—soft belly, no tenderness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t believe it. I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you with all your usual medications. No changes were made.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same doses of gabapentin and imipramine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And keep using prochlorperazine for nausea if needed. The ranitidine and cetirizine stay the same too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my GI doctor and therapist. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and we hope not to see you back here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so too. This stay really helped me reset.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. You’ll receive written instructions and a list of your meds before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll read them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your hearing aids are working okay? I tried to face you when I spoke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. Lip-reading is easier when you face me. I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Let the staff know if you need anything before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. No stress, just recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s the best medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll see my therapist next week to talk about coping strategies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great plan. Keep using your support system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve learned that ignoring stress makes the pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Mind and body are connected. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too. This stay helped more than just my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re happy to hear that. Take it easy, and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. That’s what we’re here for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home now.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a long history of chronic abdominal pain, depression, anxiety, PTSD, and hearing loss was admitted for an acute flare of her typical mid-epigastric pain and nausea. She presented with an elevated lipase of 453 but no signs of acute obstruction or gallstones on ultrasound or MRCP. Imaging showed changes consistent with chronic pancreatitis but no acute pathology. She was managed supportively with bowel rest, IV fluids, and gradual advancement from clear liquids to a soft diet. Her pain and nausea improved, and she tolerated oral intake well by discharge. All home medications, including gabapentin, imipramine, erythromycin, and hydromorphone, were continued without change. A therapist visited during admission, which the patient found helpful. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up with her outpatient providers.
